fields.definition: A harp glissando is a rapid sweep of the fingers across successive strings, sounding a run of adjacent notes; on a concert (pedal) harp the seven pedals are pre-set — often using enharmonic equivalents — so the swept strings sound a chosen scale or chord rather than every chromatic pitch.
fields.plain_english: It's the shimmering sweep you get by running your fingers across the harp strings; the harpist sets the pedals first so the whoosh lands on the right notes.
fields.purpose_function: It produces the harp's signature cascading, arpeggiated texture and lets a player sound the notes of a whole scale or chord almost instantly, an idiomatic gesture made possible by the pedal mechanism.
fields.practical_application: When recording it, an engineer captures the full sweep from the low to the high strings, watching level and stereo image so the run reads clearly and the soundboard's low-end bloom stays balanced against the string attack.
common_mistakes: Assuming the harpist can play any scale in a glissando on demand; the sounding pitches are fixed by the current pedal settings, so the wrong pedal setup gives the wrong glissando.
Miking only the top of the harp and missing the low strings and soundboard, so the sweep sounds thin and loses its bloom.
Applying a gate or heavy noise reduction that chops the natural decay and mechanism resonance which make the gliss sound continuous.
scenario_contexts: Tracking a solo pedal harp for a film score where the composer has notated specific glissando chords.
Overdubbing a harp glissando as a transitional sweep effect in a pop production.
Recording an orchestral session where the harp's glissandi must sit within the string section without excessive bleed.

fields.definition: The harp soundboard is the thin resonating wooden panel forming the front face of the harp's body, to which the lower ends of the strings are anchored; it transforms the strings' vibration into radiated sound and largely shapes the instrument's tone and projection.
fields.plain_english: It's the wooden belly of the harp that the strings pull against; like the top of a guitar, it's what actually turns the string's vibration into the sound you hear.
fields.purpose_function: By coupling the strings to a large radiating surface, the soundboard amplifies and colors the string vibrations, giving the harp its loudness and characteristic warm resonance.
fields.practical_application: Because most of the harp's radiated low end and body comes off the soundboard, engineers often aim one microphone toward the lower soundboard for warmth while a second mic nearer the strings captures attack and detail.
common_mistakes: Treating the soundboard like a guitar's soundhole and expecting one 'sweet spot'; the harp radiates over a large area, so a single close mic rarely captures the whole instrument.
Placing a mic so close to the soundboard that proximity effect and mechanical/pedal noise dominate over the strings.
Ignoring the low-frequency bloom from the soundbox, producing a boxy or boomy recording.
scenario_contexts: Choosing mic distance so the soundboard's low-end resonance is captured without becoming boomy.
Explaining to a student why the harp needs open space around its back and soundbox to project.
Diagnosing a thin harp recording that under-captured the soundboard's radiation.

sources: The Physics of Musical Instruments (Fletcher & Rossing)

fields.definition: The output of a passive electric guitar or bass (magnetic pickups, no onboard preamp) is a high-impedance, unbalanced signal whose source impedance is high and frequency-dependent, so it requires a high-impedance load — typically around 1 MΩ — to avoid loading down the pickup and rolling off high frequencies.
fields.plain_english: A regular electric guitar puts out a weak, fussy signal that needs to 'see' a very high-resistance input; plug it into the wrong low-impedance input and it goes dull and quiet.
fields.purpose_function: Passive magnetic pickups are inductive sources, so a high-impedance interface preserves their level and tone, which is why guitar amps and instrument/DI inputs present roughly 1 MΩ.
fields.practical_application: A technician routes a passive guitar into a Hi-Z instrument input or a DI box rather than a mic or line input, keeps the unbalanced cable short to limit noise and high-frequency loss, then lets the DI convert it to a balanced low-impedance feed.
common_mistakes: Plugging a passive guitar into a low-impedance mic or line input, which loads the pickup and dulls and weakens the tone.
Running a long unbalanced guitar cable to the console; high-impedance signals pick up noise and lose highs over distance, so keep the run short (roughly under 8 m / 25 ft).
Assuming a guitar's output is line level; it is instrument level and far lower, so it needs preamp gain.
scenario_contexts: Deciding whether a guitar can go straight into an interface's instrument/Hi-Z input or needs a DI.
Troubleshooting a dull, low guitar signal traced to a low-impedance input.
Setting up a long cable run from a passive bass to front-of-house through a DI box.

sources: Radial Engineering JDI passive DI technical manual
Radial Engineering technical guide: What Is a Direct Box

fields.definition: An instrument direct output (direct/DI output) is a feed that sends an instrument's signal straight to a mixer, interface or recorder — typically via a direct box that converts the unbalanced, high-impedance instrument signal to a balanced, low-impedance mic-level signal — instead of, or alongside, miking an amplifier.
fields.plain_english: It's a way to plug an instrument 'directly' into the desk without a mic, using a small box that reshapes the signal so it can travel far without picking up noise.
fields.purpose_function: It captures a clean, hum-resistant version of the instrument and lets the signal run long distances (up to about 100 m / 300 ft) without adding appreciable noise, and it can split the signal to feed both an amp and the console.
fields.practical_application: On stage or in the studio a tech plugs the bass, acoustic guitar or keyboard into a DI, sends the balanced XLR to the console for a clean channel, and optionally uses the DI's thru jack to also feed the player's amp.
common_mistakes: Confusing a DI/direct output (balanced, mic level) with a line output; plugging it into a line input yields a very low signal.
Assuming a passive DI boosts the signal; it converts impedance and balance but adds no gain, so the console preamp still supplies the gain.
Overdriving a passive DI's transformer with a hot active source and clipping it instead of engaging the input pad.
scenario_contexts: Recording DI bass alongside a miked cabinet for re-amping flexibility.
Sending an acoustic guitar's pickup to front-of-house through a DI on a live stage.
Splitting a keyboard so a clean DI feed goes to the console and a second feed goes to a stage amp.

sources: Radial Engineering technical guide: What Is a Direct Box
Radial Engineering JDI passive DI technical manual

fields.definition: An instrument headphone output is a headphone-amplifier jack on an instrument amp, modeler, preamp or interface that drives a pair of headphones for private monitoring; inserting a plug typically mutes the built-in speaker so the player can practice or track silently.
fields.plain_english: It's the headphone socket on a practice amp or modeler; plug in and the speaker usually goes quiet so you can play without disturbing anyone.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a player hear their instrument — often with amp and effects modeling — at any level without acoustic output from a speaker, and it provides a convenient monitor feed when recording.
fields.practical_application: A tech uses it for silent practice or as a scratch monitor while tracking a DI, setting a safe level for the headphones and confirming the speaker mutes so nothing bleeds into the room during a take.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: monitoring at high headphone levels for extended periods, which risks permanent hearing damage; keep levels conservative and take breaks in line with hearing-conservation practice.
Using the headphone out as a line or DI feed to a console; its level and impedance differ from a line output and can add noise or a mismatched level.
Assuming every headphone jack mutes the amp's speaker; on some devices it does not, so unwanted sound bleeds into takes.
scenario_contexts: Silent late-night practice on a modeling amp through headphones.
Using an amp modeler's headphone out as a quick monitor while tracking a DI signal.
Confirming the speaker mutes when headphones are inserted so nothing bleeds into an open microphone.

fields.definition: An instrument line output is a jack that provides a device's signal at nominal line level — professional +4 dBu or consumer -10 dBV — for connection to a mixer or interface line input, as distinct from an instrument-level, speaker-level or headphone output.
fields.plain_english: It's the 'line out' that sends a full-strength, ready-to-record signal to a mixer or interface, rather than the weak instrument-level signal a guitar puts out.
fields.purpose_function: It delivers a standardized, higher-level signal so the receiving line input needs little or no added gain, giving a clean, low-noise interconnection between pieces of gear.
fields.practical_application: A tech patches an amp modeler's or preamp's line output into a console or interface line input, matching +4 dBu versus -10 dBV levels so the signal is neither too hot nor too quiet, rather than using an instrument or mic input.
common_mistakes: Plugging a line output into a mic input, overloading the preamp and distorting; use a line input or a pad.
Ignoring the +4 dBu versus -10 dBV difference, so the level ends up too low (noisy) or too hot (clipping).
Treating a line output as a high-impedance instrument output and expecting guitar-amp tone from it.
scenario_contexts: Connecting an amp modeler's line out to an interface for a clean, DI-style record.
Matching a -10 dBV instrument line output to a +4 dBu console input.
Choosing between a line out and a miked cabinet when recording a modeler.

fields.definition: An isolation shield is a portable acoustic barrier — an absorptive (sometimes absorptive/reflective composite) panel placed around a microphone or between sound sources — used to reduce room reflections and leakage from nearby instruments during recording.
fields.plain_english: It's a padded screen you put around a mic, or between players, to block room echo and stop other instruments from spilling into the mic.
fields.purpose_function: It improves separation between sources recorded at the same time and tames early reflections, yielding cleaner, more independently controllable tracks.
fields.practical_application: A tech sets absorptive shields or gobos around a guitar amp or vocal mic, or between a harp and a nearby instrument, to cut bleed and reflections without needing a separate isolation booth.
common_mistakes: Expecting a small mic-mounted shield to fully isolate a source; it mainly reduces early reflections and modest bleed, not low-frequency spill.
Placing the shield so close that it colors the sound with its own reflections or comb filtering.
Relying on shields instead of distance, directional mics and arrangement to control heavy leakage.
scenario_contexts: Reducing bleed between a guitar amp and a vocalist tracking live in one room.
Taming a live room's reflections around an acoustic guitar microphone.
Separating a harp from other instruments in an ensemble session without a booth.

fields.definition: Leakage (also called bleed or spill) is unwanted sound from one source picked up by a microphone intended for a different source — for example, drums appearing in a vocal mic — during simultaneous recording or amplification.
fields.plain_english: It's when a mic hears things it isn't meant to, like the guitar amp showing up in the singer's microphone.
fields.purpose_function: Leakage is an unavoidable consequence of open microphones sharing a space, and it matters because it sets the limit on track separation and creates phase/comb-filtering when one source appears in several mics, so controlling it is central to clean multitrack work.
fields.practical_application: Engineers manage leakage with mic choice and pattern (directional mics with nulls aimed at offending sources), distance, isolation shields, gobos and booths, and arrangement, while weighing useful leakage that glues a live ensemble against the loss of independent control.
common_mistakes: Trying to fix heavy leakage only with a gate or EQ in the mix instead of controlling it at the source with placement and isolation.
Ignoring phase and comb-filtering when the same source leaks into several mics, causing a hollow or thin sound once tracks are combined.
Assuming close-miking alone eliminates leakage; loud nearby sources still bleed in.
scenario_contexts: Tracking a live band in one room and hearing the drum kit in the guitar and vocal mics.
Deciding mic patterns and gobo placement to minimize spill in a string ensemble.
Diagnosing a hollow combined mix caused by one source leaking into multiple mics.

fields.definition: On a stereo device, the Left/Mono (L/MONO) output is the jack designated for mono operation: when only that single jack is connected, the device provides a mono feed there, while using both jacks gives a stereo pair.
fields.plain_english: It's the 'use this one if you only have a single cable' output; plug into the L/MONO jack and you get a mono signal instead of losing half the sound.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a stereo instrument or effect feed a single mono input — an amp, mixer channel or interface input — without discarding content that would otherwise only appear on the right channel.
fields.practical_application: When a keyboard, drum machine or stereo pedal must go to one mono channel, a tech connects only the L/MONO jack as the manufacturer's manual specifies, rather than taking just the left channel and dropping right-panned material.
common_mistakes: Taking only the plain L (left) jack of a stereo pair that does not sum, which drops all right-channel content; confirm whether the jack is a true L/MONO summing jack.
Assuming every jack labeled L/MONO sums L+R; some simply pass the left channel, so behavior varies by device and the manual should be checked.
Leaving both outputs connected but sending only one to the desk, then wondering why panned parts vanish.
scenario_contexts: Sending a stereo keyboard to a single mono console channel through its L/MONO output.
Connecting a stereo effects pedal into one amp using the mono output.
Wiring a drum machine's L/MONO out to a mono DI for a live feed.
